{{Short description|Composite number with special property}}
{{Inline citations|date=September 2021}}

In [[number theory]], an ''n''-'''Knödel number''' for a given [[positive integer]] ''n'' is a [[composite number]] ''m'' with the property that each ''i''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''m'' [[coprime]] to ''m'' satisfies <math>i^{m - n} \equiv 1 \pmod{m}</math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Weisstein|first=Eric W.|title=Knödel Numbers|url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/KnoedelNumbers.html|access-date=2021-09-14|website=mathworld.wolfram.com|language=en}}</ref> The concept is named after [[Walter Knödel]].{{Citation needed|date=September 2021}}

The [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of all ''n''-Knödel numbers is denoted&nbsp;''K''<sub>''n''</sub>.<ref name=":0" />
The [[special case]] ''K''<sub>1</sub> is the [[Carmichael number]]s.<ref name=":0" /> There are infinitely many ''n''-Knödel numbers for a given ''n''. 

Due to [[Euler's theorem]] every composite number ''m'' is an ''n''-Knödel number for <math>n = m-\varphi(m) </math> where <math> \varphi </math> is [[Euler's totient function]].
